subtopic: STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO MR. DONALD GORDON, PRESIDENT

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO MR. DONALD GORDON, PRESIDENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a brief statement about the president of the Canadian National Railways. Yesterday I refrained, and I urged my colleague, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier), to refrain from any reference to Mr. Donald Gordon, because I did not believe any further discussion about his position would hasten the passage of the legislation we were considering. Certain demands have been made of the government from outside the house which I regret to say found some echo here. Therefore I believe it is in the public interest to state the position of the government.
The Canadian National Railways belong to the people of Canada^ and the only justification for their existence as a national system is the service they give to the people of the nation. The government was delighted when Mr. Donald Gordon agreed to become president, because during the war years and since he had given ample proof that he understood what was meant by putting in first place the service of the Canadian public. No doubt he would be the first to admit that he is not perfect, and that, like the rest of us, he sometimes makes mistakes; but I am convinced that every decision he has made was taken because he believed it was his duty to the public to act as he did.
In the present labour dispute the government, out of respect for the loyalty to one another of the members of the unions concerned, treated them all alike, though it was impossible to find any other vital national interest for doing so. I cannot believe that those who have been attacking Mr. Gordon really expect the government to feel any less loyalty to a faithful public servant than the members of the unions feel to one another. But lest anyone may believe we do,
I want to make it perfectly clear that the government has undiminished confidence in Mr. Donald Gordon's devotion to the public interest and in his capacity to administer the national railway system, and that we hope to see him continue to do so for a long time to come.

subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY, MOVED BY MR. CHARLES CANNON AND SECONDED BY MR. C. E. BENNETT

speechtext:
The house proceeded to the consideration of the speech delivered by His Excellency the Governor General at the opening of the session.
(Translation):

subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY, MOVED BY MR. CHARLES CANNON AND SECONDED BY MR. C. E. BENNETT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset, I wish to express my warmest personal thanks to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and those of my esteemed constituents of Iles-de-la-Madel-eine for the honour he bestowed upon me in asking me to move the address to the Governor General in reply to the speech it has pleased His Excellency to deliver before both houses at the opening of this special session.
I know that in asking me to perform this pleasant duty he wished to pay tribute not so much to myself but to the electors of the beautiful constituency of Iles-de-la-Madeleine who have endorsed the present government
[Mr. MaeNaught.I
by electing, for the first time in history, a representative of their own to the House of Commons of Canada.
I have the honour to move, seconded by the hon. member for Grey North (Mr. Bennett), that the following address be presented to His Excellency the Governor General of Canada:
To His Excellency the Viscount Alexander of Tunis, Governor General and Commander-in-Chief of Canada:
May it Please Your Excellency:
We, His Majesty's most dutiful and loyal subjects, the House of Commons of Canada, in parliament assembled, beg leave to offer our humble thanks to Your Excellency for the gracious speech which Your Excellency has addressed to both houses of parliament.
As stated in the speech from the throne, parliament has been summoned earlier than was anticipated. It was originally intended to call parliament to give consideration to certain measures for increased national security and international co-operation required by the fighting in Korea and the increasingly grave situation which that struggle reflects. We have also been summoned on account of the emergency resulting from the railway strike, which has paralysed the nation and brought about disastrous consequences that were daily growing worse.
In view of the seriousness of the times, I have not prepared a long speech and I beg to be excused if I do not make the preamble of my speech as long as is usually the case.
However, I cannot come to the heart of the matter without saying a word about the sad demises that have bereaved the country since we last separated, but two months ago.
Words fail me to describe the feeling of irreparable loss and deep affliction that gripped the whole country at the death, after a short illness, of the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King, who was prime minister of this country for a greater number of years than any of his predecessors in modern times, and who dedicated the best years of his life to the welfare of our country and the happiness of the people. The expressions of sorrow, the words of praise that followed the news of his death throughout the country and among all political parties were signal evidence of the esteem and affection in which he was held by his fellow countrymen. Even his bitterest opponents, his severest critics added their tributes to those of a whole nation. His achievements were such that the era in which he lived shall be known in the history of this country as the Mackenzie King era.

(Text):
We also have to deplore the death of Hon. Humphrey Mitchell, who was taken from us so unexpectedly. He was truly a great Minister of Labour and, particularly during the war years when his department was charged with the administration of selective service and the best utilization of the manpower of the nation, he rendered yeoman service. He was a true labour man, a member of the trades and labour congress and the holder of a card in the electricians' union. He knew our workingmen, particularly our union men in Canada, and his wise counsel will be sorely missed, particularly in trying times such as those through which we have just passed.
(Translation):
We also mourn the death of the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Belzile), parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). Elected for the first time in 1945, he distinguished himself rapidly in this house and was on his way towards achieving a brilliant parliamentary career. Never was his star so bright, and death, in taking him away from us, has deprived the country of a son who was capable of rendering great public service.
I join with those who have already expressed their sorrow and sympathy at the passing of these great men.
(Text):
I wish to underline the appointment of Hon. Milton F. Gregg to the important portfolio of labour. This portfolio is always an important one, but it is particularly so at this time. May I say that it is universally recognized as a great compliment to the minister that he should have been appointed under the circumstances that existed at the time.
(Translation):
I wish to offer to the Hon. Hugues Lapointe my most sincere congratulations and those of my constituents on his appointment as Minister of Veterans Affairs. He was clearly designated to this office by his remarkable service record in France, Belgium and Holland during the last war. The worthy son of an illustrious father, he will no doubt follow his example and walk in his footsteps.
I am just back from my constituency of Iles-de-la-Madeleine where I spent some time with my family.
In general, fishing has not been good this year. The lobster catch was satisfactory, but cod and mackerel were not profitable
The Address-Mr. Cannon during the months of June and July on account of the bad weather, which disturbed the fishermen during the greatest part of these months.
Fishermen's income has been severely cut; as they rely on this income to buy the fuel and food they need for the winter months, and fishing gear for next season. The fishermen of the Magdalen islands, who represent 85 per cent of the population, find themselves in a difficult position which could even become distressing. They have already forwarded to the hon. Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew) several requests in which they set out their problems and their needs. I have given my support to those requests and although fisheries in the province of Quebec come under the provincial authorities I am convinced that the federal government will take, if need be, the necessary steps to prevent the Magdalen islands fishermen from suffering from cold and hunger next winter.
This special session was called first of all to allow parliament to consider the necessary steps to provide for our national security which is jeopardized by the ever-increasing menace of communism and to let the members decide to what extent we must co-operate with the United Nations forces now fighting in Korea to defend the Korean republic against their sinister and brutal aggressor.
But before the opening date of the session had been set, we met with a domestic crisis which threatened the security and welfare of the nation in a more direct and urgent way than the other crisis. It is more pressing to settle our own affairs than to re-establish peace elsewhere.
The railway strike which has just ended was a menace to our national life and threatened the vital forces of the nation by stopping the circulation in its arteries: the railways.
Every Canadian was worried, anxious even. Our people were appalled at what was happening. They were confronted with a situation they would never have thought possible. Some time ago, in the last days before the 22nd of August, the date set for the strike, the level-headed and experienced citizens thought that there would not be a strike. They said: "Labour unions and the railways are managed by men of wisdom and of real ability, by good Canadians who will, on both sides, make the necessary concessions to avoid such a national disaster."
Evidently they were wrong. The necessary mutual concessions were not made. There was no sign of that breadth of outlook which

The Address-Mr. Cannon would have put the welfare of the country before that of the unions or the companies. The disaster was not averted but was permitted to take place regardless of the consequences for the country.
Most of the railway employees, I am sure, were surprised and disappointed when the strike was launched. Many of those who had voted in favour considered their vote merely as a threat which was not to materialize but was meant only to force the hand of the companies.
The public does not feel secure any more. What monstrous power, they ask, has made it possible for a few men, for a very small percentage of our population, to paralyse the economic life of the nation, to isolate whole communities, to deprive sick people of medical care, children of their milk, the merchant [DOT] of his legitimate profit, their brother workers of their livelihood and their wages in many industries affected by the strike? The Canadian citizen feels it is time to put a stop to this power, to regulate this force which is unable to control itself.
Public opinion did not support the strikers; it was not a popular strike. Even the man in the street, who has not studied philosophy, with his plain common sense, realizes that public interest must prevail over private interests. The parties concerned are blamed especially for their refusal to postpone the strike for thirty days, as had been suggested by the government, in order to settle the dispute. It was thought that a delay of thirty days was not overly long, and could have been granted in order to avoid this disaster.
I am sure that the organizers of the strike had no intention of fostering communism, because I know that their leaders are strongly opposed to communism. Nevertheless, if communists could have brought about a similar strike they would have considered it a tremendous victory. They would have welcomed a strike that paralysed the main transportation services of the country, namely the railways which brought Canada into being. We all know that without the railways confederation would never have been achieved. They were one of the main conditions of union between the eastern and the western provinces.
Let us remember that the eyes of the world are focused upon us; everywhere, people have been wondering how we would tackle the problem. The eyes of the sovereign people -the masters of our democracy-are also turned towards us, awaiting a fair, equitable and impartial solution to this stalemate. In the province of Quebec, public opinion has


already accepted legislation forbidding strikes in public utilities. In 1944, the legislative assembly of that province passed a bill decreeing compulsory arbitration in every dispute over labour conditions where a public utility and its employees were involved and rendering illegal any strike in a public utility under any circumstances whatsoever.
Heavy penalties are provided in this legislation for every day that such an illegal strike would last. This law is still in force and has given good results. It was enacted by a Liberal government known for its sympathy towards organized labour.
However our federal government did not want to incorporate this principle into the labour legislation of this country. It did not want to enact general legislation prohibiting strikes in public utilities and subjecting them to compulsory arbitration.
In Bill No. 1, introduced in this house last Tuesday, and subsequently carried, this government has found, and of this I am convinced, a fair solution to an immediate problem.
The Liberal party still believes in the principles of collective bargaining and free arbitration, but, all efforts at conciliation and arbitration having failed in this particular case, it was absolutely necessary to find a way of getting the railways back into operation.
The government has found a way through this act, which orders the railway companies to return to the operation of their lines and subsidiary services and orders the railway employees now on strike to return to work. The act grants all employees a temporary wage increase of 4 cents an hour, and provides that, if within thirty days after the act has come into force, management and labour have not yet reached an agreement as to the terms and conditions of the collective agreements covering their jobs, or on the appointment of an arbitrator to determine such terms and conditions, the governor in council will appoint an arbitrator. The arbitrator will rule on all matters on which agreement has not been reached and which must necessarily be settled if a collective agreement is to be drawn. His decisions will be binding on the employees and on the companies. If he grants other wage increases, these will be retroactive at least to the date on which the workers will have resumed work following the passing of the bill I have just mentioned.
As Mr. St. Laurent pointed out in this house, this law does not introduce the principle of

compulsory arbitration in our labour laws. A specific case had to be settled, a national crisis had to be stopped by means of a special law which applies to that case only.
This law does not infringe upon the freedom of the unions which all Canadians cherish; it does not encroach upon their right to strike. This right is recognized in all democracies and I hope it will always be in Canada.
This law is based upon two principles. First, pressing too much for private rights may lead to public wrong; then the rights of each must be limited by the rights of others. The abuse of one's rights must be stopped.
When the exercise of a right causes more harm to the community than the limitation or restriction of this right would bring to some groups, that right must be restricted.
Such is the object of that legislation. It is in force only in so far as it is necessary to ensure the resumption of railway operations and the settlement of the present emergency.
Here I wish to congratulate the government for having summoned the houses of parliament to deal with this problem. That the government did not wish to make these grave decisions without consulting the elected representatives of the people is an example of true democracy in action. Our opponents often criticize the government for governing by order in council. Our presence here today is the answer to these accusations: the facts speak for themselves.
I am happy to see that nearly all our colleagues are here today. I am sure the people realize the difficulties the members of parliament had to overcome and the personal sacrifices they had to make to get here in spite of the strike. The leader of the opposition is probably the one who came from the farthest point. I am sure I speak for all members in saying that we appreciate the difficulties he had to overcome in order to be with us today.
The speech from the throne also states, Mr. Speaker, that we have been summoned here in order to find means for bolstering our national security against the threat of aggression which has arisen in the east and of strengthening the international co-operation required by the fighting in Korea and the increasingly grave international situation which that struggle reflects.
(Text):
Canada, Mr. Speaker, is a member of the United Nations. She signed the United
The Address-Mr. Cannon Nations charter in 1945, and this signature was ratified by both houses of parliament. Under the charter Canada has assumed obligations toward the other signatory nations. She has agreed to take effective collective measures for the suppression of acts of aggression, to give the United Nations every assistance in any action they take in accordance with the charter, and to accept and to carry out the decisions of the security council, also in accordance with the charter.
The security council has passed three resolutions in connection with the Korean situation by which it has declared that there exists a breach of the peace in Korea, has branded the North Koreans as the aggressors, and has recommended, under article 39 of the charter, that all member nations assist in the defence of the republic of Korea. This is the first time in history that Canada has bound itself by covenant to give armed assistance to any nation, whether inside or outside the British commonwealth of nations.
There is no possible doubt that this undertaking was approved and wholeheartedly ratified by the people of Canada. Canada was represented at the San Francisco meeting and at the signing of the charter by our Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent); and the people of Canada have shown their entire approval of what he did there, as Secretary of State for External Affairs, by electing him Prime Minister by the greatest majority in the history of this country.
This is also the first time that Canada has been called upon to honour its signature to an agreement to give armed aid to another nation. Are we going to honour our signature? I say, yes. We are not going to fail this first test; and I am sure this house will also answer the question with a resounding yes, authorizing the government to send the special force to Korea or to use it to fulfil any of our other obligations under the United Nations charter or the North Atlantic treaty.
In the last days of the last session, Mr. Speaker, the Korea question was before this house, and members of all opposition parties expressed their support of the decision our government had taken to support the United Nations resolution recommending that the members of the United Nations furnish such assistance to the republic of Korea as may be necessary to repel the armed attack and to restore international peace and security in the area.
There is also the further consideration that it is only fitting that this country should equip and send to Korea as a fighting force
86	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Cannon those of her sons who generously volunteer to go and defend the citizens of Korea against the barbarous aggression they are now suffering.
May I interject here, sir, that it was with regret that I read recently in the newspapers that the hon, member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) has called upon the veterans of Canada not to volunteer for service in Korea and has also called upon the government of this country to establish conscription for this service. The hon. member is taking a course which is entirely illogical. Experienced, trained and willing troops are needed in Korea. He dissuaded the experienced, trained and willing soldiers from volunteering, and suggested that raw recruits, without experience or training and without even the desire to enlist for this action, should be forced to go. If he had set out deliberately to weaken and sabotage the special force, he could not have done more to attain that end.
I have suggested, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member for Kamloops has been illogical.
I think I can support that statement with an example taken out of yesterday's proceedings. Several times he voted against what he termed compulsion to oblige men to accept a determination of an increase in wages of between four cents and seven cents an hour. He was against compulsion in that case, yet he would use compulsion to send young men to risk their lives in Korea when Canada is not even at war. But fortunately he has not succeeded in so weakening the special force. As you know, sir, the recruiting of volunteers has been going admirably well and has already exceeded the number of men originally set by the government.
This spontaneous movement of our youth to join the special force being organized under the auspices of our able Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) shows their confidence in him and their satisfaction with the splendid work he has done in unifying the command of the three forces, in reorganizing, modernizing and co-ordinating our defence headquarters. The unification of our three services has progressed unobtrusively, without fuss or controversy, in a manner that is the envy of other nations that have not been so fortunate, and we now have, or so we are told by representatives of other nations, one of the most modern, best trained, best co-ordinated and integrated defence headquarters machines of any nation west of the iron curtain.
In support of the resolution of the United Nations concerning assistance to the republic of Korea, Canada had already sent into action three destroyers. It is worthy of note that the


first armed forces of Canada to take part in this fighting belong to the service in which the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Langlois), whose county then included the Magdalen islands, served in the last war. Canada has also sent a number of transport planes of the R.C.A.F. which are participating in the airlift to Japan. Our rearmament is going apace. Large orders for aircraft and the most modern guns have been placed, and arrangements have been made to train in Canada 300 aircrew a year for the United Kingdom, France, The Netherlands, Belgium, Italy and Norway. I wish to take this opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to congratulate the Minister of National Defence on these splendid achievements.
(Translation):
That rearmament program, on which I have just congratulated the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton), will enable us to fulfil in various parts of the world the obligations imposed upon us by the United Nations charter and the Atlantic pact. All of it will not necessarily serve only in Korea. We may have to ward off threats from elsewhere. Although part of our national wealth must be earmarked for our rearmament program, we must not neglect the general strength of our economy or the welfare of our people. Nothing would please communists better than to see our people unhappy and divided. We must prevent that at all cost, as such a situation could serve the purpose of the enemy.
We are fighting this war on two fronts: the theatre of operations in Korea and the United Nations arena at Lake Success. I wish to take advantage of this opportunity to express my most sincere appreciation to the hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs, to the various Canadian delegates to the United Nations assembly, and also to the representatives of the great democracies, namely, France, Great Britain and the United States, for their excellent work in this arena in answering the deceitful allegations of those who support the aggressor and exposing the falsity and weakness of their arguments.
The forces of good must, now more than ever, join hands to fight the forces of evil. It is comforting to see fifty-three of the fifty-nine United Nations denounce the aggressor in Korea and to see that an ever-increasing number of nations are offering to send reinforcements to United Nations troops.
Let us ask ourselves if these great democracies should not hold out a friendly hand to Spain and if Canada should not lead the way

in this direction. I am not speaking of the United Nations since any step in that direction at the United Nations level would inevitably meet with the customary veto. The Senate of the United States made a friendly gesture towards Spain when it voted that country a loan recently.
It seems to me that in rejecting an alliance with that country against communism we deprive ourselves of an ally that could be very useful in certain circumstances.
I am sure that in passing Bill No. 1 yesterday this house took a step which will put an end to the national paralysis caused by the railway strike.
I am no less certain that this house is ready to take the necessary steps in the international sphere to maintain that degree of cooperation required to deal with the very serious situation now existing.
There is no doubt in my mind, Mr. Speaker, that in doing these things the representatives of the Canadian people in the parliament of the nation will receive the full support of their fellow citizens. Our people wish that all the necessary steps be taken for the preservation of order in this country, that public interests be protected against the self-centred and unconsidered actions of a few and that Canada with all the strength of a young nation having recently reached new heights in independence and autonomy respect her undertakings and honour her obligations.
