speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxton (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY, MOVED BY MR. CHARLES CANNON AND SECONDED BY MR. C. E. BENNETT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you and hon. members have just heard from the Secretary of State for External Affairs a masterly exposition of the international situation, and against that background scene, it now becomes my duty to describe what we Canadians are doing in consequence of that situation. We heard it from the lips of our own Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) speaking with directness, frankness and eloquence that has made him known in the council chambers of the world, and round the world too. He has raised high the name of Canada around those council tables in the work for peace just as other Canadian ambassadors in the forces of our country, on occasions grim and serious, painted the name of Canada in golden letters for all the world to see, admire and respect.
It is my very great privilege to congratulate the mover (Mr. Cannon) and the seconder (Mr. Bennett) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. The mover, with a distinction indicating that he is a worthy son of a highly respected father, dealt with a good many of the topics that I have to tackle today. The seconder went even further, and on the basis of his own exceedingly distinguished war service, in which he attained the rank of group captain, he also dealt with a good many of such matters. I think the hon. member for Grey North (Mr. Bennett) is now the senior ranking air force veteran in the house. I have no doubt that in matters of defence we shall receive from him the same kind of constructive help as every veteran, including the dean of them all,

The Address-Mr. Claxton the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes), has given in the discussions that have taken place here.
As I was preparing my speech last night, Mr. Speaker, the radio was turned on for the national news bulletin. One could imagine people listening in from Grand Falls in Newfoundland, from Estevan, Rimouski and Niagara Falls, people who were glad that the trains were rolling again. Then I heard Mr. Frank Hall and Mr. A. R. Mosher come on the air and in level tones full of responsibility tell the men that the law would be obeyed. It was a most striking demonstration of the democratic process, of the rule of law, of the power of parliament and of the good sense of the Canadian people. All who were in this chamber yesterday will remember yesterday as one of the great days of parliament. Here was parliament acting in very reality as the grand forum of all the people.
I dare say other members felt the same way as I did about it, but more than ever I felt yesterday a sense of the solidarity of parliament irrespective of party, place, race, language or religion. We were meeting as Canadians to tackle a most difficult problem. It was the job of the members elected by the people to work on that problem having regard to the interests of all concerned, having regard to conditions, but above everything else having regard to the greater interest of all the people of Canada. The attendance of members in the house, coming from different parts of the world in such numbers, showed our sense of the responsibility and importance of the moment.
I could not help feeling how Mr. King, who was a great parliament man, would have liked to see this triumph of the parliamentary system. He would have liked to see the knowledge, good sense, transparent honesty and capacity of his great successor and also, if I may say so, his great patience. I can assure hon. members that this country has been fortunate in having as its leader the present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) throughout the railway crisis. He was the leader of us all, and I venture to say that at every stage he knew more about all sides of the question than anyone else knew about their own side. It was his knowledge as well as his wisdom that brought us through to the beginning of what we hope will be the successful termination of a very difficult question.
Then it seemed to me last night that the broadcast brought home the amazing unity and sterling qualities of the Canadian people. They accepted the challenge and the added difficulties brought about by the strike with good heart and good humour. There was

little bitterness or rancour. There was great resilience, resourcefulness and capacity for improvisation. It was this kind of quality in the Canadian people, in the workings of our parliamentary democracy, which showed us why we must be prepared at any and every cost to defend our country. We are determined that we and not the communists shall rule Canada. That this will require sacrifices is evident.
The events of the last few months have shown that the communists are prepared to run great risks to extend the sweep of the iron curtain. It is sometimes said that democracies have a choice between guns and butter. For me there is no choice. We must continue to develop our resources, expand our economy, extend the area of all the freedoms within the nation, and at the same time with other nations meet the threat of aggression by the one thing that will stop it, trained united strength. Business as usual is not enough. We are going to have more business than usual, much more business than usual for everyone. To remain free we must work to strengthen our democracy on every front, from attack from within and from without. All this is going to require fortitude and anyone who thinks that we can do it without hurting ourselves is out of step with the march of events.
The events of yesterday demonstrated another thing. I believe, strong in my belief in the Canadian people, that, just as our forefathers did in pioneering this country, just as others did in the first and second world wars,, just as we have done in the magnificent recovery and grand achievements of the last five years, just as the Canadian people have met the challenge of the strike, just as they have met so far the challenge of Korea, there is no people better qualified to meet the challenge of events, no matter what they may bring, than the people of Canada. The work we have done in the armed forces to get the accelerated program going, and the splendid response to the highly successful recruiting campaign, have shown that we are facing up to the job.
When the special force was announced by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) on August 7, as provided by P.C. 3860, there were some who said it would not work, that it was the wrong way to do it, that this and that were wrong about it. Within two weeks the special force had been recruited; most of it is already equipped and at work in the training camps, surprisingly fit and ready to go on with the accelerated training program; as fine a group of men as I have ever seen. What is more, during the same period we

have taken in enough men to provide reinforcements for the first year. Now they are all off to attend our fine training camps at Valcartier, Petawawa, Shilo, Currie and Wainwright, and at the specialist schools, getting on with the job.
This was a considerable exercise in mobilization. It worked well, but we learned a lot. I have teams of people at work going over the experience of the last few weeks, trying further to streamline procedure. I can say, though, that should an emergency arise we know how many men for each of the three services we shall want during each of the first twelve months. We know what kind of men they should be, what they will do, where they will go, what they will be equipped with and how they will be trained. That is all taped down to the last man. Those figures and these plans are subject to constant revision; and of course in consequence of our experience when a job of ten per cent or fifteen per cent or twenty per cent or thirty per cent mobilization was carried out we learned a great deal about how further to streamline the procedure. By and large, however, I think the administrative machinery here worked in a way that showed it was adaptable, because it could do the special job of raising this special force in these special circumstances.
This was a special job; as has been pointed out by each of the three previous speakers, it was not part of the planned role of Canada that we should have standing by a full-time professional force ready to police the farther parts of the world. That is not ordinarily the role of a medium-size nation, and it was not the planned role of Canada. It was no part of our defence program; there was no promise that it would be done, and there was no suggestion that we should prepare to do it. As the hon. member for Grey North (Mr. Bennett) said, our forces were prepared for two eventualities; first, to defend our own country against direct attack; second, to build up an all-out effort in a total war. As a matter of fact events have shown that no country, not even the most powerful nation on the face of the earth, our good neighbour the United States, was prepared for Korea. Suggestions have been made that we should have sent the airborne brigade group of the permanent force. On August 7 the Prime Minister explained why we did not think that should be done. The brigade group, we believe, is as highly trained as any force of its size anywhere in the world. They are trained for the special purpose of defending this country. They are airborne, and in Exercise Sweetbriar they showed that they could live and fight and 69262-71
The Address-Mr. Claxton work in the Arctic. I do not think anyone has seriously suggested that this force should be sent out of the country. It is worth noting, though of course this may not remain the case, that so far corresponding elements in the United States forces are still in the United States.
So the special force was decided upon; and as I have indicated, it was quickly raised. As at the close of business last night we had recruited a total of 8,272 for this force. The three infantry battalions are over strength, but that does not mean we have all the men we want for all three, because we are continuing to recruit reinforcements sufficient for the first year and we also need certain classes of men, particularly tradesmen, for the other units in the force. In addition, of course, we are continuing to press on with recruiting for the active forces of the navy, army and air force. So let no one think that because we have recruited the strength of the special force and three thousand reinforcements as well, we are stopping there either for the special force or for the active force. We are pressing on with both, and we shall need additional men out of new recruits in certain categories for the special force.
All the senior officers have been chosen, and the evidence of their fighting records is exemplified in the na'tion-wide reputation of their commander, Brigadier John M. Rockingham, C. B. E. and a double D. S. O. In no case was a unit commander a second choice. The rest of the officers are being speedily chosen. The total number of this force, including first echelon reinforcements, as now planned will be 6,775. It will consist of units which will include three battalions of infantry, a regiment of artillery, a squadron of self-propelled guns, and elements of engineers, R.C.E.M.E., medicals and all the other branches of the service necessary to constitute a self-contained group. In addition there will be over 3,000 replacements.
This force is being supplied with the equipment we have, which generally speaking is of the United Kingdom type. In addition we are acquiring some new types of weapons particularly for this force. We are quite prepared to have it work under the United Nations banner with other forces similarly equipped, or to have it integrated with United States forces and supplied with United States equipment if this course later appears desirable.

subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY, MOVED BY MR. CHARLES CANNON AND SECONDED BY MR. C. E. BENNETT
speechtext: What about a commonwealth division?

subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY, MOVED BY MR. CHARLES CANNON AND SECONDED BY MR. C. E. BENNETT
speechtext:
The equipment of United
States pattern will be needed for the United States forces, however, and probably it

The Address-Mr. Claxton would take longer for us to be able to use such equipment, so at the present time we are planning on the use of equipment of the United Kingdom type. As to the question of a commonwealth division, we believe all the forces fighting in Korea should be known as United Nations forces. The United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand have offered ground forces, and already some of those of the United Kingdom have arrived. No doubt they will have equipment of the United Kingdom type, as we expect to have. If it is considered desirable by the unified command that the part of the United Nations forces having equipment of the United Kingdom type should work together in a division which would include the components of the British commonwealth and any other countries that may be fighting there with British type weapons, we would be quite prepared to undertake that course or to adopt the alternative. We want to do whatever makes the most sense from the point of view of being co-operative and making effective use of the forces we have.
The position of Canada of course has got to be such-it is unfortunate or perhaps it is fortunate-that we have to be prepared to work with one or the other of these types Of equipment for some considerable time to come. In the past we have shown we can do it to a considerable degree, and we shall continue to do it in the future. Logically perhaps the objective should be that the countries of North America should use North American type equipment, but that time is still a considerable distance away. While the objective will be worked at, it certainly cannot be achieved in the immediate future.
This force will have included in it a substantial element of the active force, artillery, self-propelled guns, signals, engineers and so on. Altogether more than a thousand officers and men will be posted from the active force to the special force. I should like to emphasize here that there is no difference between the two. They are both components of the Canadian army active force. They serve under identical conditions of service, except that the special force has a term of service of eighteen months, or longer if required, and will also have advantages similar to those enjoyed by the forces that were overseas during the second world war.

subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY, MOVED BY MR. CHARLES CANNON AND SECONDED BY MR. C. E. BENNETT
speechtext:
Are the thousand men to
whom you referred included in the eight thousand you have already mentioned?

subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY, MOVED BY MR. CHARLES CANNON AND SECONDED BY MR. C. E. BENNETT
speechtext: No.

subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY, MOVED BY MR. CHARLES CANNON AND SECONDED BY MR. C. E. BENNETT
speechtext: That is in addition?

subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY, MOVED BY MR. CHARLES CANNON AND SECONDED BY MR. C. E. BENNETT
speechtext:
That is right. They are quite apart from the 8,272 already recruited and under training, but they will be included in the 6,775 strength of the special force and the
3,000	or more reinforcements earmarked for the force.
This group of a thousand from the active force will represent something like twenty per cent of the effectives of the special force, and about twenty-five per cent of the brigade group. Their places will be speedily filled in the brigade group to bring the active brigade group up to full fighting strength.
Owing to a number of circumstances such as the high proportion of trained men from either the active forces or veterans-the proportion of veterans is over forty per cent- the method of training adopted and the quality of the rest of the men, this force will be trained months ahead of the time it would ordinarily take for freshly recruited men. We expect the force will be through basic and advanced training so that it can move on to unit and brigade training ten weeks from now. As the Prime Minister stated on August 7, the Canadian army special force will, with the approval of parliament, be available for service in Korea as part of the United Nations forces if it can be most effectively used in that way when it is ready for service.
In answer to the member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), it is not exclusively earmarked for use with the United Nations. It may also be used in any action undertaken by Canada under the North Atlantic treaty, and is of course always available for the defence of Canada, which is included as one of the purposes of the North Atlantic treaty.

subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY, MOVED BY MR. CHARLES CANNON AND SECONDED BY MR. C. E. BENNETT
speechtext: When is it likely to be ready for service?

subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY, MOVED BY MR. CHARLES CANNON AND SECONDED BY MR. C. E. BENNETT
speechtext:
That could not be estimated at this time. It would depend upon the time it would take to get them to a place of training, the weather there, the type of training required, the availability of equipment, and half a dozen other considerations. It would be within a matter of several weeks or a few months.
In addition to the special force, we have been pressing on with recruiting to fill up all the ranks of the special force and also to add new anti-aircraft batteries. Between July 20 and August 30, we have taken in 401 men for the navy, 1,412 men for the active force of the army, 218 aircrew and 281 ground crew, making 499 for the Royal Canadian Air Force, or a total of 2,312 for the active force which, with the 8,272 for

the special force, makes a grand total of 10,584 men. On June 30 the ceilings for the three forces were 50,912 and their strengths were 46,899. We have increased the ceilings by forty per cent for each of these forces, bringing them to a total of 69,160 of which we now have 56,962. We shall be further increasing the ceiling for the army. Naturally, our plans provide for a balance between the anticipated flow of men, the personal equipment to fit them out, the barrack accommodation, the capacity of the training establishments and, finally, finished equipment such as ships and aircraft.
At the present time we have in training as officers, to what I believe are as high standards as there are anywhere in the world, a total of about 6,000 men.
We want this flow of recruits to continue. I should like to say that there is no advantage whatever in further reducing standards. While we are doing a lot of in-service training and giving a lot of education in the service, we cannot do much more because it takes too long, costs too much and uses up available manpower that might be used for other purposes. With regard to the standards of R.C.A.F. aircrew, I have seen some suggestions that we have too high a rate of rejection. I looked into this myself in Toronto on Saturday at the institute of aviation medicine. I went over the selection procedures with the specialists there, and I believe it is generally recognized that in this field Canada is one of the leading countries in the world. We developed that position before the war, continued and extended it during the war, and have increased it since. I am prepared to show hon. members who would be interested that if we increased the proportion of men taken into the air force as aircrew it would result in one of two things, neither of which is desirable.
First, it would reduce standards, and we mean to have the highest standards in the world for aircrew. Second, it would mean that a very high proportion, as high as one hundred per cent of the lower groups of men taken in, would not be able to complete their course. This has been carefully worked out and it is possible to estimate in advance with complete accuracy the proportion of men of each standard who will graduate and become successful aircrew. In view of the high cost of training aircrew, probably more than $25,000 or $30,000 per man, in view of the waste of their time and effort involved-our aim is to get just as high a proportion of the men through as possible-we believe that the high standard of entrance is good economy so long as we can get the men of the high standards we
The Address-Mr. Claxton desire. We want also more tradesmen for all three services, more men having considerable education wiho can maintain and use the highly complex equipment of the modern forces.
So far I have dealt with this program largely from the point of view of manpower, because that is what counts in the end. However, the finest men need the finest equipment, and that is what we are trying to get them. The accelerated program, as announced day by day since July 20, includes a large speed-up in the planned rate of production. We have nine ships in construction for the navy: an Arctic transport icebreaker, three anti-submarine vessels, four minesweepers and a gate vessel. The navy is furnishing today about half the work being done in Canadian shipyards. We are pressing on with that program and we are going to add more anti-submarine vessels and more minesweepers. The maritime commission and the Canadian Commercial Corporation are working on the rate of production and the numbers. All the ships will be the last word in vessels of their type.
We shall be putting into commission every ship in the navy as men are trained and the ships are successively modernized. The program, already well advanced, of modernizing the armament, equipment and accommodation on all the ten destroyers is being speeded up. We shall be fitting on each the latest three-inch, 50-calibre gun, to be made in the great gun plant at Sorel by Sorel Industries Limited, under arrangements with the United States navy. The antiaircraft armament and anti-submarine armament are steadily being modified to include the latest developments. We shall also be adding _ greatly to the existing stocks of ammunition for the navy. We have arranged to purchase twelve Sea Furies for the Magnificent, thus providing a reserve for operations at war strength on the carrier until the year 1952.
Work has been begun in enlarging the accommodation at the fine training establishment at Cornwallis in Nova Scotia and also in other essential places. The test of this work in the navy lies I think in the fact that at the present time nearly fifty per cent of the personnel in the navy is at sea. That is a remarkably high proportion of naval personnel in any navy to be at sea. As we know, the three destroyers are at Korea where they are giving a good account of themselves.
I should place on Hansard a signal from General MacArlhur reading as follows:
On behalf United Nations delighted to accept force under your command for service in repelling aggression in Korea. The proposed sailing schedule indicates prompt action and readiness of the R.C.N.

The Address-Mr. Claxton
That was sent to the chief of the naval services.
With regard to the army, there seems to be some thought that the army is getting the thin end of the'stick with regard to equipment. I can tell you that the chief of the general staff and his advisers do not hesitate to put forward requests for what they feel it is advisable for them to have. Those requests are considered and acted upon as is the case with the other services. The army, however, is in a special position. We have in mobilization stores or on issue a large part of the equipment required, if we had to get into a war, for the first year of that war. Some time ago the number of items of equipment was given to me as totalling 121 million out of 182 million that were needed for that period.
Fewer new developments of army equipment have been brought into quantity production in most countries than in the other services since the war. We shall be adding steadily to anti-aircraft and anti-tank weapons, partly by making modifications which will give us the latest development in radar, predictors, et cetera, as well as new weapons. We shall also be acquiring considerable quantities of ammunition and motor vehicles. We shall be tooling up for the manufacture in Canada of new types of military motor vehicles. For the army we shall need considerable additions to accommodation to look after the increased numbers and replace buildings that have long outlived their life expectancy.
Then in addition to the active force, we are looking forward to a considerable increase of numbers and activities in the reserve force of all three services but particularly the army. At the present time the reserve forces of navy, army and air force total 50,000. They have had a good summer's training. They have good equipment. We are improving the accommodation and we shall be putting on a major program of recruiting beginning in September, at the commencement of the training period, so as to add substantially to the strength of the reserve forces, particularly the reserve army.
It is, however, in the air force that the most spectacular figures are shown because aircraft cost so much money. Since parliament last adjourned, Canadair Limited produced the first F-86 to be made in Canada, which I saw flown in August, right on the planned schedule. We have doubled the planned rate of production of these aircraft and have placed an order which the press have cleverly calculated as being more than three hundred, for what I think is one of the largest single orders ever placed toy anyone in Canada in war or in peace, representing over $100 million. The
CF-100, the "Canuck", is under production at A. V. Roe (Canada) Limited, .at Malton, and here we are also doubling the planned rate of production.
These two aircraft are, we believe, the best aircraft there are in their respective fields and together will give Canada a team which we believe will not be matched in any other country in the world. Both aircraft will be eventually powered by the Orenda engine and there we have increased the planned rate of production of this engine fivefold. We believe that this engine will prove to be one of the most powerful and efficient jet engines yet to be produced. Equipped with these engines, the "Canuck", two-engine, two-seater jet, will be powered by the equivalent of more than 15,000 horsepower.
Last week we arranged to purchase 100 Mustangs from the United States so as to provide additional combat strength for our squadrons until they can be equipped from our own production. This arrangement, like all others, indicates the way in which the United States works with us and we with the United States in a close working partnership not only for the defence of North America but in our work together under the North Atlantic treaty.
We have under way a large program for continued modification and reconditioning of aircraft we already have. We shall need all these to meet the accelerated training program for our own aircrew for which we shall want an intake of 25 every week, and also we shall need this additional equipment to do the job of training we have undertaken for other countries.
When I was on the other side in November, I initiated discussions with the defence ministers of the other countries working together to ascertain if they would be interested in training aircrew and army officers in this country. The offer was well received and today we have here, or will have soon, aircrew in training from France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Norway and Italy. We may have other countries represented later. Further, however, I know that hon. members will be more than glad to know that we have arranged also to train 150 pilots and 50 navigators for the United Kingdom. The British commonwealth air training plan was one of the greatest paths to victory. In it there were trained 131,000 aircrew of the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia and New Zealand. Seventy-one thousand were Canadians. Now we have made similar arrangements not only with the United Kingdom but with other countries as well so that we can get the pattern of action going and the procedures lined up to do the job on a much larger scale should that prove to be necessary.

It was fitting that the discussion I began of this co-operation with the United Kingdom should have been with my friend, the Right Hon. Arthur Henderson, and that it should have taken place last September at the Trenton gate ceremony, which, you will remember, commemorated the establishment of the British commonwealth air training plan. The first group of twenty-five aircrew will arrive on January 15, and will be followed by similar groups every six weeks. In addition, the air force has a very large schedule for production of radar and wireless equipment, and that of course is being pressed on and expanded. Here again in the air force we are adding very considerably to the number of reserve units, and a new radar unit will be established in Toronto in September, with later radar units in Vancouver, Halifax and other places, following the very successful formation and recruitment under Wing Commander Patrick of the unit at headquarters in Montreal, but extending to most of the province of Quebec.
It is interesting to note that the performance of the air force is shown not only by their fine record in war and in peace, but tlso in their work in the 426 squadron which was dispatched to Korea. I have here a message just received, referring to that work, from General L. S. Kuter, commanding general of the United States air force M.A.T.S. It reads:
The accomplishments of the R.C.A.F. squadron delivering tonnage to the Far East have been noted with pleasure, particularly when compared with the squadron commitments. The 426 transport squadron is to be congratulated on the fine effort produced to date in the Korean airlift.
If time permitted I should like to mention a good many other matters in connection with defence. Industrial organization of course is one which comes into great prominence at this time, when we are so expanding the production of the country. That comes under my colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), who will be telling you later of the arrangements that have been worked out with the United States for the resumption of our very close co-operation in this field during the last war. This will result in the planned use of the industrial resources of both countries with defence purchases being at least roughly balanced on a reciprocal basis. Up to now, since the war, we have been buying a good deal more equipment from the United States than the United States has been purchasing from us. As everyone knows, our productive capacity is very great indeed. Seventy per cent of everything we made during the last war went to other countries.
The Address-Mr. Claxton
We can produce almost anything and do it as efficiently and economically as any country. Today that productive capacity is to a large extent working full time on civilian supplies. We shall, however, be placing very considerable additional orders for the supply of new equipment made in Canada not only for ourselves but also for assistance in western Europe under the North Atlantic treaty.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) has mentioned the fact that we would be extending this assistance. This is not the time to deal with it in detail because the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) will be introducing a bill to provide for additional appropriations for the armed forces, and also to provide assistance under the North Atlantic treaty. It is at that time that the matter may be gone into at greater length. But here I would indicate, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs has already done, that this is part of the planned program, and I can assure hon. members that the amount of assistance that will be made available will be very substantial indeed.
In connection with the North Atlantic treaty, I think I might mention seven ways in which we are working together. In the first place, with regard to defence planning, this is being done both on a regional basis and for all the twelve nations. In the second place, we make our primary contribution to the North Atlantic treaty organization in seeing to the defence of Canada. In the third place, we also co-operate with the United States in planning and carrying out arrangements for the defence of North America as a member of the North American group, and also with the other ten nations involved in the north Atlantic ocean group. In the fourth place, we have made these offers which have been so gladly accepted for training aircrew and army officers. In the fifth place, we are cooperating exceedingly closely with the other nations in the exchange of information, development of weapons and the like. In the sixth place, we are making this very substantial offer of equipment, which will be dealt with more fully later this session. And finally, there is the all-important question of morale, of moral support, of indicating that this is an unlimited partnership.
When the Minister of Finance presents his appropriation bill I think hon. members will see that the expenditures of Canada will compare very favourably on any basis with those of the countries of western Europe, and that by and large on most bases of comparison the only countries that will exceed Canada proportionately will be the United States and the United Kingdom, and even in those cases the gap will be very considerably narrowed.

The Address-Mr. Claxton
All this of course will cost a great deal of additional money. Before dealing with that I might also briefly mention the question of defence research which is being expanded. Here, as in the case of the other services, the expenditure is on personnel, equipment, laboratories, and buildings. We are continuing to give special emphasis in the fields in which Canadian experience has made notable contributions in the past, namely, ballistics, explosives, propellants, high-speed aerodynamics; combustion in jet engines, cold weather operation of aircraft, aviation medicine, defence against biological and chemical warfare and many other interesting and some intriguing and some rather nasty topics.
What we have been doing in regard to defence research is to have people who are outstanding in their respective fields do work which enables us to put our share of knowledge, experience and development into the pool of new ideas.
In connection with civil defence, last week the ministers and officials representing the provinces met here, and in accordance with previous discussions we agreed to lines of co-operation. The first representatives of the provinces will be attending two courses opening at Borden in September.
As must be evident to hon. members, all this will cost a great deal of money. This year the vote by parliament in June provided for a cash appropriation of $425 million. The estimated cost of that part of the accelerated program which will require cash expenditures this fiscal year-that is up to the 31st of March, 1951-is another $140 million to $150 million. For next year it will, we estimate, be something in excess of $225 million, and probably very much more in excess of that, with a similar amount for the third year; and that of course assuming that the present planned strengths, rate of production, program of construction and so on remain about the same.

All additional, and quite apart from any assistance to the North Atlantic treaty nations.
If the international situation demands it, we can accelerate this program by getting more equipment sooner, doing more construction, provided the money is available, and that will require of course much greater expenditures and even larger inroads in the civilian economy. With virtually full employment, and the highest gross national production in our history, we are at a point where any additional production means that the inflationary tendency will be very considerable, and also means that there will not

be manpower, material or productive equipment, except by cutting the civilian economy.
Because of what has happened there have of course been developments in every country along lines similar to our own, and where the legislatures have been in session there have been discussions and reports similar to those taking place today. We have followed these with great interest. When the roll is called and the accomplishments are known, I think it will be found that the degree of increase and acceleration of our program will have enabled us to say that we have done a job and played our part.
In conclusion I think we can say that we have been fortunate in that we were able to complete the post-war organization of the armed forces earlier and to a greater extent than most other countries, so that we have a sound organizational foundation upon which to build. It is, I believe, a smoothworking and efficient set-up, well trained, loyal, with high professional attainments and high standards of service. This organization has been carried through without recrimination, resignation or reversals of policy.
We have established uniform conditions of service with food, pay, pensions, clothing, hospital services, married quarters and all the conditions of personnel service on a basis comparing favourably with good civilian standards.
Before Korea this resulted in our being able to recruit steadily to meet planned requirements. After Korea, because of the foundations laid, it was possible to start the accelerated program in a matter of hours.
Another thing, we have had throughout and in every way the closest possible cooperation of the most satisfactory character with the United States and the United Kingdom, as well as all the countries of the commonwealth and all the countries in the North Atlantic treaty.
We have, I believe, as high standards as any country for our officers, and we have a comprehensive organization for training officers and men to the high standards we want and get. In the all-important field of aircraft development we have produced two of the finest aircraft in their field in the world, as well as a most powerful engine.
What is more, the armed forces have shown the qualities we would like to see them have in their work.
I need only remind hon. members of rescue operation "Canon", the splendid exploit of the Haida rescue, the Fraser valley and Manitoba floods, the Rimouski and Cabano fires, Exer-

cise Sweetbriar and the three destroyers and the transport squadron winging their way to the Far East.
But perhaps most important of all, we have .created to a greater degree than I believe in any other country the sense of loyal unity between officers and men of the navy, army and air force at every level and in every branch, between active and reserve forces and, to an extraordinary degree, between the services and the civilian community.
The old attitude there used to be toward sailors and soldiers is a thing of the past. Our sailors, soldiers and airmen have attained and earned the respect of the community. And I believe that the community, speaking through members of parliament, will support the armed services and the government in the great strides we are making in step with the other free nations of the world to show that vigilance is the price of freedom, and to pay the price so that we in our own beloved country shall continue to call the tune.
